dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment

evidence.note: Orients to the environment first — inspects /app, Python version, installed packages, and the empty scaffold before building; establishes what's available.
Discovers via testing that the real Stripe SDK uses HTTP Basic auth (key:''), not only Bearer, and revises auth.py — a genuine SDK-grounded contract correction.
Installs the actual `stripe` SDK and points it at the server, using real SDK round-trips to confirm compatibility of the main resources.
SDK sends nested form encoding items[0][price]; agent discovers its parser mishandles list indices and fixes it mid-build — reconstructing SDK wire behavior as a gap surfaces.
Probes the hard parts — webhook re-signing per attempt (notes timestamp/replay-window semantics), idempotency replay of cached decline error bodies, 4xx-stops-retry — grounded in observed behavior.

Object shapes, error envelope, test PANs, and error codes are all written from memory with no external/doc source consulted; fidelity of codes/PANs never verified against authoritative Stripe references.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it establishes the core contract for main resources and confirms SDK auth handling (correcting Bearer→Basic), and it probes all four hard parts (idempotency scope, webhook re-signing, PI state machine, restricted keys) grounded in real `stripe` SDK round-trips, revising design mid-build (auth, form parsing) as gaps surface. It falls short of anchor 8's full 'systematically probes grounded in how the real API behaves,' because the reconstruction is memory-driven with SDK round-trips only confirming parseability — the test-PAN set, error codes, and decline_code shapes were never checked against documented Stripe semantics. That places observed behavior at a 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps

evidence.note: Recognized scale ('This is large. Let me plan') and decomposed into dedicated modules (ids, cards, errors, store, webhooks, auth, utils, server) — a structured breakdown, but organized around code modules, not an ordered milestone hierarchy with done-conditions. Traps (webhooks, idempotency) got their own modules, so they weren't buried in CRUD.
Got a bootable, auth'd skeleton verifiable early (health endpoint, then Bearer+Basic auth) before layering resources — an 8-flavored 'skeleton first' trait.

Each of the three named traps received its own explicit check: idempotency replay incl. error-body replay, PI state-machine unexpected_state, webhook retry-on-5xx/stop-on-4xx/re-sign. Treated as distinct workstreams with dedicated verification.

Late edge-case sweep (list filters, deleted resources, restricted-key reads) was reactive ('let me re-review before marking complete') rather than driven by a pre-declared milestone acceptance list; done-conditions were emergent, not planned up front.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent exceeded a flat checklist (anchor 5): it verified a bootable auth'd skeleton early and treated the three traps as distinct workstreams, each with its own module and explicit verification check. But it fell short of anchor 8's deliberate risk-aware sequencing — there was no explicit ordered milestone plan with pre-declared per-milestone done-conditions or dependency articulation; the structure was module-first with emergent, test-driven done-conditions. That interpolates to a 6.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks

evidence.note: Boots service, curl health + customer create; testing surfaced the Bearer-vs-Basic auth gap, which the agent then fixed — verification driving design, not just 'returns 200'.
Targeted trap checks: idempotency replay, card decline (4000000000000002), invalid PAN rejection, and capturing twice -> payment_intent_unexpected_state state-machine error.

Installed and drove the real `stripe` SDK against the local server (as the verifier does); through it found a subscription items[N][price] form-parse bug, fixed utils.py, and re-tested — regression caught rather than assumed.

Webhook delivery verified with a custom short STRIPE_WEBHOOK_RETRY_SCHEDULE: retry on 5xx, re-sign each attempt, stop on 2xx/4xx; noted same-second-timestamp limitation for late re-sign but did not actively test a late-delivery accept window.
Covered error envelopes (401 no-auth), restricted-key scoped permissions, list pagination/limit, and customer delete — broad envelope/HTTP-mapping coverage.

Concurrent same-key idempotency serialization was reasoned from the code ('my entry-level lock serializes, good') rather than exercised with actual concurrent requests — the main gap short of a full level-10 harness.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent verified through the actual `stripe` SDK against api_base and built specific checks for every named trap — idempotency replay including a cached decline body, invalid PAN decline, capture-succeeded -> 400, and webhook 5xx retry/backoff/re-sign — plus pagination, restricted-key permissions, error envelopes, and a re-test after fixing a bug the SDK exposed, comfortably clearing the level-8 anchor. It falls just short of 10 because the hardest concurrency trap (serialized same-key retries never double-charging) was reasoned from the lock design rather than exercised concurrently, the late webhook re-sign accept-window was noted-but-untested, and tests were ad-hoc scripts rather than a persistent re-runnable harness. That places the observed behavior at 9.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface

evidence.note: Agent works through the surface in a mostly systematic order (customers, PMs, PIs, decline, invalid card, state machine, SDK compat, subscriptions/invoices/webhooks/restricted keys), demonstrating awareness of what has and hasn't been exercised, without an explicit checklist artifact.
Discovered a form-parsing gap for subscription items, diagnosed root cause and fixed it in a single pass, then re-ran — no repeated/circular re-debugging of the same case (no thrashing).

Before finalizing, the agent lists remaining edge cases to verify (missing auth, restricted-key permission, deleted resources, list limit/pagination, customer delete shape) and reallocates attention to cover them rather than over-polishing one area.

Final enumeration accurately maps coverage against the full route table and all three trap subsystems (idempotency error replay, webhook retry+re-sign, PI unexpected_state), showing an accurate done-vs-remaining picture at close.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an accurate mental picture of coverage across all 12 resource families and the three traps, moved through them without leaving major areas silently unstarted, and showed no circular re-debugging — matching and slightly exceeding the level-5 anchor. It falls short of 8 because tracking was implicit prose rather than an actively maintained checklist against the route table, and it never explicitly time-boxed a stuck behavior (it never got stuck) nor clearly distinguished implemented-only from implemented-and-verified. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures

evidence.note: Discovered via curl -u that the Stripe SDK uses HTTP Basic auth (key as username) while the service only accepted Bearer; recognized the contract divergence and rewrote auth.py to support both — a fix on the central auth path applied across all routes, not a single endpoint.

Subscription create failed because SDK sends items[0][price]=...; diagnosed the underlying form-parser model (couldn't index numeric list keys) and rewrote _set_path to handle lists generally, then restarted and re-tested — a root-cause structural fix affecting all nested-list params.

Observed identical signatures on webhook retry attempts, reasoned about the second-resolution timestamp cause, and correctly judged it acceptable for late deliveries — evidence-driven interpretation rather than reflexive patching.

The three deep traps (idempotency error-replay, webhook 5xx retry/4xx-stop/re-sign, PI unexpected_state) passed on first verification, so no structural pivot of those subsystems was triggered — limiting demonstration of the level-10 'structural pivot' behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent hit two real SDK-contract divergences (Basic-vs-Bearer auth, bracketed-list form encoding), treated each as a signal about the external contract rather than a surface bug, fixed the underlying model, and propagated the fix across the affected surface — matching anchor 8. It falls short of 10 because the deep trap subsystems were validated correctly on first attempt and thus never demanded the structural pivots the top anchor describes; the corrections observed, while root-cause and well-propagated, were on peripheral plumbing rather than the risk-heavy subsystems.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity build: a single-container service that emulates the Stripe REST API at the wire level, faithful enough that the real `stripe` Python SDK works unchanged. Difficulty comes from breadth (12+ resource families, list/error envelopes, restricted keys) AND depth on three explicitly named traps with subtle concurrency/temporal semantics (idempotency replay incl. cached errors and same-key serialization, webhook retry/backoff/re-signing, PaymentIntent state machine), all offline against an external contract the agent must reconstruct. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep research of the real Stripe contract, milestone decomposition across a large surface, SDK-driven verification, progress tracking, and course-correction when compatibility breaks.

dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment
dimensions.description: Understanding the externally-defined Stripe wire contract (resource shapes, error codes, test PANs, list/idempotency/webhook semantics) and the SDK's expectations before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is really the real Stripe API; fidelity is graded against SDK behavior the agent must infer, not against this prose. Guessing field names, error codes, or the test-PAN set produces silently non-compliant output.

anchors.0: Starts coding straight from the prompt; invents field names, error codes, and PANs with no reference to actual Stripe behavior.
anchors.3: Recalls a few Stripe shapes from memory; covers the obvious resources but leaves error envelope, list envelope, or PAN set half-guessed.
anchors.5: Establishes the core contract for main resources — object shapes, error `{type,code,...}` mapping, list envelope, the published test-PAN set — and confirms how the SDK sets `api_base`/auth headers before building on them.
anchors.8: Systematically probes the contract for the hard parts too: idempotency key scope `(api_key, key, body)`, webhook signature format, PaymentIntent status transitions, restricted-key scopes — grounded in how the real API/SDK behaves, and revisits sources as gaps surface mid-build.
anchors.10: Sustained, self-correcting reconstruction: cross-checks each subsystem's behavior against concrete SDK round-trips or documented Stripe semantics, catches under-specified corners (decline_code vs code, replay of cached error bodies, re-signing for replay windows) early, and lets findings reshape the design rather than discovering mismatches late.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into an ordered hierarchy — auth/boot skeleton, CRUD resources, then the risk-heavy idempotency/webhook/state-machine subsystems — each with a clear done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is too large to hold in one push, and the three named traps carry most of the risk; a flat, breadth-first slog will run out of horizon before the hard semantics are correct.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between endpoints ad hoc with no ordering or done-conditions.
anchors.3: A flat endpoint checklist with no risk prioritization and no explicit 'done' criteria per item.
anchors.5: Clear milestones (boot+auth first, then resource groups, then the traps) with rough done-conditions, and recognizes the three traps as distinct workstreams.
anchors.8: Risk-aware sequencing: gets a bootable auth'd skeleton verifiable early, then deliberately front-loads or ring-fences the high-risk subsystems (idempotency serialization, webhook backoff/re-sign, PI state machine) as first-class milestones each with an explicit check, rather than burying them in CRUD.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that visibly de-risks the whole horizon: dependencies made explicit (e.g. PaymentIntent charges before refunds before subscription invoices), the trickiest semantics scheduled while budget remains, and the plan carries concrete acceptance conditions per milestone that later verification maps onto.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing how correctness is confirmed — exercising routes with the real `stripe` SDK / requests, and building targeted checks for idempotency, webhook retry, and state-machine edge cases — beyond 'it returns 200'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Wire-level compatibility and the trap semantics fail silently; only active verification (ideally through the SDK the way the verifier will) distinguishes a plausible-looking response from a compliant one.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because the code was written.
anchors.3: Manual curl of a couple of happy paths; no SDK check, no coverage of error bodies or the trap behaviors.
anchors.5: Boots the service, smoke-tests health and several CRUD flows, and checks a few error/edge cases — but leaves the hardest semantics (concurrent idempotent retries, webhook backoff, illegal state transitions) largely unverified.
anchors.8: Verifies through the actual `stripe` SDK against `api_base`, and constructs specific checks for the traps: replaying an idempotency key (incl. a cached error body), same-key-different-body → 400, capturing a succeeded intent → 400, invalid PAN → decline, webhook 5xx retry/backoff.
anchors.10: A deliberate verification harness that covers happy paths, error envelopes, HTTP-code mappings, list pagination, restricted-key 403s, and the concurrency/temporal traps (serialized same-key retries never double-charge, re-signed late webhook deliveries), re-run after changes so regressions are caught rather than assumed away.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture over 12+ resource families and the trap subsystems, and detecting when effort is stuck or circling on one behavior.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With this much surface it is easy to lose the plot — over-polishing customers while subscriptions/invoices/webhooks remain unstarted, or re-debugging the same idempotency case repeatedly.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; forgets whole resource families or repeats work.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; discovers late that major endpoints or the webhook worker were never implemented.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of endpoints/subsystems and their status, and generally knows what remains.
anchors.8: Actively maintains coverage against the full route table, notices when stuck on one behavior and time-boxes it, and reallocates attention so no major area is silently dropped.
anchors.10: Continuous, accurate accounting across the whole horizon: distinguishes implemented-and-verified from implemented-only from missing, catches thrashing/circular debugging early and names it, and adjusts pace to land the full surface plus the traps within budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when SDK round-trips, error shapes, or trap semantics diverge from expectations — rather than pressing on with a falsified assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reconstructing an external contract guarantees wrong initial assumptions (field names, signature scheme, state rules); the agent must let contradicting evidence rewrite the design, sometimes structurally (e.g. how idempotency serialization or the billing worker is built).

anchors.0: Ignores failing SDK calls or wrong outputs; keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Patches surface symptoms (tweaks a field) without revisiting the underlying wrong model, so the same class of mismatch recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the root cause for that case and moves on.
anchors.8: Treats divergences as signals about the contract: on discovering e.g. a wrong signature format or state-transition rule, updates the mental model and propagates the fix across related endpoints, not just the one that failed.
anchors.10: Fluid, evidence-driven correction across the horizon, including structural pivots when needed (rethinking idempotency locking, webhook re-signing, or state-machine modeling once reality contradicts the plan), while preserving already-verified work — never barrels ahead on a falsified assumption.
